item.title: The quest for a quieter Dhaka. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The government’s decision to tighten noise pollution rules -- including a ban on honking in residential areas from 9pm to 6am and stricter limits across silent and industrial zones -- is certainly a welcome step.
Dhaka has long been ranked among the world’s noisiest cities, and the consequences of unchecked noise pollution have never been taken into consideration - which is a mistake.
Noise pollution affects productivity, mental well‑being, and overall public health and basic livability of the capital. For a city that continues to be ranked as among the least liveable cities in the world, even a small improvement in curbing noise pollution will be seen as a win. We are also a city already struggling with air pollution, traffic congestion, and urban chaos. As such, ignoring noise is no longer an option.
News laws set clear decibel limits, restrict high‑noise equipment, prohibit the manufacture and sale of illegal horns, and empower traffic sergeants to impose on‑the‑spot penalties. All of this, on paper, is positive.
However, these measures will only have any impact if we see enforcement. Dhaka has seen rules before, and most have collapsed in practice. As such, regulations are needed -- but they must be backed by real consequences and not just laws for the sake of laws.
Dhaka’s noise crisis is not entirely solvable, but we can make some progress to reducing it. For that to happen, the government must treat it with the seriousness it deserves and actually follow through with implementing the rules it sets. The task is to enforce consistently and finally give residents a city where some quiet is not a luxury.

item.title: Harnessing our greatest asset. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On International Youth Day 2026, Bangladesh is reminded once again that while young people grow up in vastly different circumstances, their aspirations converge.
Whether in Dhaka’s dense urban neighbourhoods or in rural districts where opportunities remain scarce, the hopes of Bangladesh’s youth are strikingly similar: Dignity, opportunity, safety, and a future they can shape rather than inherit passively.
We saw this in our very recent history as the youth of this nation spearheaded the Monsoon Revolution of 2024, and it is this energy that we are failing to capture as a nation when it comes to developing our nation for the better.
This year’s theme for International Youth Day - “Different Contexts, Common Aspirations” - is particularly significant for us.
Our young people continue to navigate unequal access to education, uneven digital connectivity, and sharply contrasting economic realities. They share the same desire for an education system that prepares them for real work, not rote learning; a job market that rewards skill, not patronage; and institutions that listen to them rather than dismiss their concerns.
Bangladesh’s youth have been central to political movements, climate activism, social justice campaigns, and digital innovation. They have pushed institutions to be more accountable and demanded that leaders respond with clarity rather than complacency.
Their energy has never been the issue - the issue is that our systems remain too slow, too rigid, and too outdated to match them.
International Youth Day is a reminder that Bangladesh’s future depends on whether it can turn the shared aspirations of its young people into real progress. Different contexts may shape their lives, but their hopes are aligned, and their expectations, rightfully, are rising.
Bangladesh must do better to meet those expectations. We cannot afford to waste our greatest asset.

item.title: Sheikh Hasina’s virtual press conference, and plausible deniability. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The textbook definition of plausible deniability is the ability of a person, often a high-ranking official, or organization, to deny knowledge of or responsibility for controversial, illegal, or unethical actions because there is a lack of clear, conclusive evidence connecting them to the act.
It ensures that leaders remain officially uninformed or disconnected from risky operations. The definition is further expanded to say that in such situations, communication is often kept vague, implicit, or unwritten (such as verbal nods or winks) so that subordinates carry out tasks without a direct paper trail.
If the operation is exposed, leadership can credibly claim ignorance and shift the blame downward to "rogue" agents or lower-ranking staff. Traditionally it is used by governments undertaking covert actions abroad so the state or executive can disclaim responsibility if operatives are caught.
The recent press conference held by the former prime minister of Bangladesh (referred to as virtual because she participated in it through audio call) under the auspices of the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of New Delhi, is a flagrant example of plausible deniability by no less an authority than the government of India.
The Indian government has officially denied any involvement in this press conference of so-called foreign correspondents calling the entity a private organization.
How private or how foreign is this organization?
The Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia (FCC) is based in New Delhi and is often referred to as the Foreign Correspondents' Club of New Delhi. It is a club of more than 500 journalists and photographers covering India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Bhutan, Nepal, Maldives, Afghanistan, and Tibet.
The club web page says, while the club was started by "foreign" correspondents, or those who work for news outlets outside of the region, it also welcomes journalists from local newspapers, magazines, and television. It also admits associate members such as diplomats, lawyers, and people dealing with the media from NGOs and companies.
In other words, the Foreign Correspondents’ Club is as foreign as all residents of New Delhi. The 500 or so members include some foreign journalists, but the overwhelming number are Indian journalists. Its executive committee mostly comprises Indians.
For example, its current president is Syrian-born Waiel Awwad, but an Indian national, and Secretary Prakash Nanda, another Indian journalist.
The August 5 audio press conference was titled "Bangladesh at the Crossroads" -- also promoted as "Save Democracy in Bangladesh." The invitation card identified Hasina as "The Honourable Prime Minister of Bangladesh" even after her ouster, which drew attention in Dhaka.
How credible is it that an entity of such a huge number of journalists who are Indian nationals can hold a political conference with a fugitive political leader of another country without knowledge or clearance from the government?
Was it a political masquerade, or sheer disregard of any fallout from a weaker neighbour, for allowing this event to take place in the lair of government?
The purpose of this article is not to debate whether or not Indian authorities had a priori knowledge of the press conference. The press conference was advertised by the Indian media and reflected in Bangladesh long before it took place.
If an ordinary person knew about it, it is common sense that the Indian authorities also knew about it.
Both the organizers and the chief guest participating virtually were doing it from Indian soil, a stone’s throw from South Block, administrative headquarters of the Indian government.
The Indian government had both the power and wherewithal to prevent this provocative conference if it had wanted to.
Instead, it chose the traditional political ploy of deniability because the conference was organized by a private entity.
This took place despite pleas from Bangladesh that allowing the former PM to address journalists is giving her a political platform which will severely jeopardize the already fragile relationship between two countries.
This press conference, where Sheikh Hasina made political statements, happened despite the official position that India has taken regarding her stay in India.
Officially, she is not a political asylee as Indian law does not allow asylum. In its report 'The Future of India-Bangladesh Relationship' chaired by Congress MP Shashi Tharoor, it was stated : "The former prime minister of Bangladesh, Sheikh Hasina, stays in India on humanitarian grounds however, the government does not provide her with a political platform or any space to undertake political activity from Indian territory."
It described the formula as: “Humanitarian refuge, no political space.”
Despite this “official position” of India that Sheikh Hasina is in India on humanitarian grounds, with no political space, the press conference was allowed to take place and Sheikh Hasina announced her political plans to the world.
This is from a person who has been convicted of crimes against humanity by the country she fled from. The Indian government may hide behind plausible deniability, but Sheikh Hasina has proved that she could use her shelter as a political space, contrary to assertion by the Indian parliament.
Sheikh Hasina’s press conference proves two things. She is not retiring from politics anytime soon, and she intends to retain the leadership of her party. But there is a gap between her desire and reality.
The reality is that the anger and outrage against her 16-year rule which led to her ouster is still prevalent in the country. However defiant she may sound when she declares that she will return to the country to challenge her conviction, she will also have to reckon with the anger of the population.
Sheikh Hasina was in total control of her party while she was in power. But that party is broken in pieces with its members running helter skelter.
Despite being the oldest political party of the country, the organization has suffered badly from the Hasina effect which not only tarnished her image but also many of its leaders.
Her statement in the press conference that she will return to Bangladesh sounds like empty rhetoric given that her own party is unable to rally around her now.
Ziauddin Choudhury has worked in the higher civil service of Bangladesh early in his career, and later for the World Bank in the US.

item.title: What is the SSC result really telling us?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest SSC results tell us something that is easy to miss if we look only at the pass rate or the number of GPA-5s. They tell us less about how much Bangladeshi students are learning and more about how the country has gradually changed the meaning of examination success.
This year, 62.25% of students passed the SSC and equivalent examinations, the lowest pass rate in 19 years. In 2007, the combined pass rate was 57.37%.
At the same time, 116,676 students achieved GPA-5 this year, compared with 139,032 last year. The decline may appear alarming, but perhaps the more important question is not why fewer students obtained the highest grade. It is why we became so accustomed to enormous numbers of GPA-5 holders in the first place.
The history of GPA-5 provides an uncomfortable answer. When the grading system was introduced in 2001, only 76 students obtained GPA-5. The number rose to 330 in 2002, 1,392 in 2003, 8,597 in 2004 and 17,631 in 2005.
By 2010, the figure had reached 52,134. In 2014, it crossed the 100,000 mark for the first time, reaching 142,276. Eight years later, in 2022, it peaked at 269,602. This year, it stands at 116,676.
The numbers are extraordinary. But they should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that Bangladeshi students suddenly became dramatically more capable.
A GPA is ultimately a measurement produced by an assessment system. If the assessment system changes, the meaning of the number changes with it.
A country can produce more GPA-5 holders without producing a proportionate increase in critical thinking, creativity, communication skills, or intellectual independence.
That distinction lies at the heart of Bangladesh's education problem.
For years, we have treated examination results almost as a national performance index. A high pass rate is celebrated as progress. A record number of GPA-5s becomes a source of institutional pride.
Newspapers publish lists of successful students. Families celebrate. Educational institutions advertise their achievements. But almost nobody asks the more difficult question: What can these students actually do with what they have learned?
The supplied data itself suggests why such a question is necessary. Educationists argue that even if every student passes an examination, that alone cannot establish the quality of an education system.
Quality depends on teaching methods, institutional facilities, and the competence of teachers. Those structural weaknesses, according to the experts cited in the source, remain unresolved.
This means the latest SSC result should perhaps be read not as a report card of students, but as a report card of the system that teaches and assesses them.
The rise of GPA-5 also coincided with a broader transformation in the educational landscape. The number of colleges, universities, and educational institutions expanded. Admission became increasingly competitive. Results became an important currency for students, institutions, and policy-makers.
In such an environment, examination statistics can acquire a political and institutional importance that goes beyond measuring learning.
The problem becomes particularly visible when the pass rate itself becomes an objective.
If institutions need students, if colleges need enrolment and if educational expansion creates pressure to demonstrate success, there can be an incentive to make the statistics look healthier.
The source material points to concerns among education researchers about over-marking, changing question patterns, shortened curricula, flexibility in assessment, and political pressure.
Some researchers have even argued that past governments had reasons to inflate pass rates and GPA-5 figures to demonstrate educational success.
Whether every such claim is correct is less important than the larger institutional question it raises: Are we designing education around learning, or are we designing learning around results?
The distinction matters because the SSC examination is not merely an academic milestone. It determines much of a student's immediate educational future.
Class XI admission is based on SSC GPA and marks, with students competing for preferred colleges through an online merit-based process. SSC and HSC results are also used in university admission requirements, scholarships, and technical education. In some cases, SSC results remain relevant to employment eligibility as well.
So the pressure to obtain a high GPA is entirely rational from a student's perspective.
But that is precisely where the system can become dangerous.
When a single examination determines access to the next stage of education, students naturally learn to optimize for the examination.
Parents demand marks. Teachers concentrate on likely questions. Coaching centres sell shortcuts. Students memorize answers. Institutions compete over GPA-5 statistics.
Learning can then become secondary to scoring.
The consequence is a peculiar contradiction. Bangladesh can produce hundreds of thousands of students with the highest possible school grade while simultaneously worrying about the quality of teaching, teacher preparation, institutional capacity, and students' actual learning.
The problem is not that students are achieving GPA-5. The problem is that GPA-5 has become too weak a proxy for educational quality.
The figures from the last 25 years make this contradiction particularly visible. From just 76 GPA-5 holders in 2001 to 269,602 in 2022, the system experienced an almost unimaginable expansion in the production of top grades. Yet there is no equivalent evidence in the supplied data showing that the country experienced a comparable transformation in teaching quality, educational infrastructure, or learning outcomes.
The pendulum is moving in the opposite direction
GPA-5 numbers have fallen from 269,602 in 2022 to 183,578 in 2023, 182,129 in 2024, 139,032 in 2025, and 116,676 this year. The pass rate has also fallen significantly. This could represent a crisis. But it could also represent an overdue attempt to make assessment more credible.
A stricter examination is not necessarily bad news.
If fewer students pass because the system is finally demanding genuine mastery, the decline should not be treated as failure.
Failure would be to maintain impressive statistics while students leave school without the ability to think independently, communicate effectively, solve unfamiliar problems, or apply knowledge beyond an examination hall.
The real danger, therefore, is not a falling GPA-5 rate. It is our continued obsession with the GPA-5 rate.
Bangladesh needs an education system in which examination results are evidence of learning, not substitutes for it.
A student who scores 95 but cannot write a coherent argument, analyze information, or communicate an original idea should force us to question the system, not simply congratulate the student.
The latest SSC result may therefore be portraying a country caught between two educational models. One model measures success through numbers, rankings, pass rates, and GPA-5s. The other asks whether those numbers represent genuine intellectual development.
The first model is easier to advertise.
The second is much harder to build.
Perhaps that is why the latest SSC result should not be read simply as a story of falling pass rates and fewer GPA-5s.
It should be read as a warning that Bangladesh has spent too long asking how many students passed and not enough time asking what they learned.
If the answer to that question remains uncertain, then even 269,602 GPA-5s are not proof of educational success. They are merely 269,602 numbers printed on certificates.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.description:
International standards are often assumed to be a modern invention. They are not. Many predate the United Nations itself; the International Labour Organization (ILO), for instance, was established under the League of Nations and only later folded into the UN system. Countries have long used such standards to strengthen governance, build credibility, and integrate into the global economy.

Pakistan has been one of them.

Over the decades, it has voluntarily become a party to numerous international treaties and conventions, incorporating many of their provisions into its Constitution, national legislation, and regulatory framework, including constitutional guarantees relating to fundamental rights, labour protections and environmental governance.

It is, however, worth remembering that joining an international treaty is a sovereign, voluntary decision. Pakistan took on these obligations because they were seen as consistent with its long-term development goals, not because it was compelled to.

Today, the country is party to well over 150 major international treaties, conventions, and protocols spanning governance, trade, labour, human rights, environmental protection, maritime affairs, and more.

Far from being symbolic, these commitments strengthen market access, attract international investment, support development cooperation and trade negotiations, and reassure global buyers about the credibility of Pakistan’s regulatory framework. Many of them, notably, were undertaken decades before concepts like ESG, carbon border measures, and supply-chain due diligence became central to global trade.

The labour record: ahead of the pack

Pakistan’s commitment to international labour standards illustrates this long-standing pattern well. The country has ratified 38 ILO conventions and one protocol, including eight of the 10 Fundamental Conventions — covering the abolition of forced labour, minimum working age, freedom of association, collective bargaining, equal remuneration, non-discrimination, and the elimination of child labour.

The remaining two — Convention No. 155 on Occupational Safety and Health and Convention No. 187 on the Promotional Framework for Occupational Safety and Health — are currently under active consideration for ratification. Pakistan has also ratified two of the four ILO Governance (Priority) Conventions, on labour inspection and tripartite consultation.

Why does this matter? Because labour standards increasingly determine market access, particularly for export-oriented economies in Asia.

Pakistan has also ratified the Protocol of 2014 to the Forced Labour Convention, signalling its commitment to global best practices and reassuring international buyers that its exports meet internationally recognised labour standards. Tellingly, India has not yet ratified this protocol, despite its labour-related commitments under its free trade agreement with the European Union. Several major Asian textile and apparel exporters — including China, Vietnam, and Cambodia — have not ratified it either, despite being far more deeply integrated into global value chains than Pakistan.

Beyond labour: environment and the wider picture

Labour is only one part of Pakistan’s broader compliance landscape. The country is also party to 15 major Multilateral Environmental Agreements (MEAs), covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, hazardous chemicals and waste management, ozone layer protection, desertification, and cultural and natural heritage.

The scale of this engagement becomes clearer when viewed over time. The chart below traces the cumulative growth of Pakistan’s international commitments since independence and it shows a country that has, year after year, steadily expanded its participation in international legal frameworks.

Committing to international standards is no simple undertaking. Ratifying a treaty is only the beginning; it requires governments to review their domestic legal framework and, where necessary, amend legislation, strengthen institutions, and align national policies with international obligations.

Pakistan’s 18th Constitutional Amendment, for example, devolved many environmental and labour-related responsibilities to the provinces, creating an extensive compliance architecture that runs from federal ministries down to provincial departments and, ultimately, local governments.

The challenges are real

None of this has been easy, and challenges remain. Even the world’s most advanced economies have yet to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals; Pakistan is no exception.

Part of the reason is that many international standards are negotiated and implemented within sophisticated legal and regulatory systems that are more readily supported by advanced economies. Less developed economies, by contrast, often face additional implementation hurdles owing to resource constraints and competing development priorities.

These challenges are compounded by Pakistan’s geopolitical environment. Sharing borders with India and Afghanistan, the country continues to contend with persistent security concerns and regional instability, adding further pressure on its institutions.

Despite these constraints, Pakistan has repeatedly shown a willingness to update its compliance frameworks in line with emerging global expectations.

International law keeps evolving in response to new global challenges, geopolitical developments, increasingly stringent trade rules, and more complex global value chains.

Most recently, in response to concerns raised by the United States over the risk of forced labour in global supply chains, Pakistan promptly amended its Import Policy Order to prohibit the import of goods produced wholly or partly using forced labour, well before India or Bangladesh adopted comparable measures. As a result, imported products containing inputs produced through forced labour at any stage of the value chain are now barred from entering Pakistan’s market.

The story behind the numbers

The graph above tells only part of the story. Behind every point on it lie years of negotiations, legal reforms, institutional strengthening, and policy decisions. Their impact is rarely visible overnight, but none of that work has gone to waste.

Perhaps it is time to recognise that Pakistan’s engagement with international standards is not a recent phenomenon. It has been quietly laying the foundations for sustainable development for decades.

And this is the Pakistan we must not overlook.
